title: Why eigenvalues exist
objectives: Prove that every operator on a complex finite-dimensional space has an eigenvalue.

screens.title: Push one vector
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 0)$. The canvas draws $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (2, 1)$. Apply $\mathbf{A}$ once more.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{A}(2, 1)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $\mathbf{A}$ by $(2, 1)$: each entry is a row of $\mathbf{A}$ dotted with $(2, 1)$.

byKey.double: You doubled $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$. $\mathbf{A}$ is not $2\mathbf{I}$: the off-diagonal 1s mix the entries.
byKey.swap: You swapped the entries. The first row $(2, 1)$ dotted with $(2, 1)$ gives 5.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}(2, 1) = (5, 4)$. Now we have three vectors $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v}$ in the plane. Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ cannot be independent.

screens.title: Three vectors in a plane
screens.prose: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are dependent (level 1 l3). So $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} = a\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{v}$ for some $a, b$. Move the sliders until the blue arrow $a\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{v}$ lands on $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} = (5, 4)$.
screens.question: What are $(a, b)$?

hints.text: The second entry of $a(2, 1) + b(1, 0)$ is $a$.
It must equal 4, the second entry of $(5, 4)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second entry of $a\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{v}$ is $a$ alone. Start there.

byKey.signs: You moved the terms across: $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} - 4\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + 3\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ has $-4$ and 3. The question asks for $a, b$ in $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} = a\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{v}$.
byKey.swap: You swapped $a$ and $b$. The multiple of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ comes first.

explain.text: The second entries give $a = 4$, then the first gives $8 + b = 5$, so $b = -3$. So $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v} - 4\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} + 3\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. A polynomial in $\mathbf{A}$ sends $\mathbf{v}$ to zero.

screens.title: A polynomial that kills v
screens.prose: So $p(z) = z^2 - 4z + 3$ has $p(\mathbf{A})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. It factors as $(z - 3)(z - 1)$, so $(\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I})(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Call $\mathbf{w} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}$.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{w}$?

hints.text: Its first column is what it does to $\mathbf{v} = (1, 0)$.

byKey.three: You used $\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I}$. The factor applied first is $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{I}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w} = (1, 1)$, and $(\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I})\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$ because $p(\mathbf{A})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. If $\mathbf{w} \ne \mathbf{0}$, it is an eigenvector for 3. The factors of $p$ point at the eigenvalues.

screens.title: The arrow that stays on its line
screens.prose: The canvas applies $\mathbf{A}$ to the arrow $\mathbf{x}$, and the band is the line of $\mathbf{x}$. Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{w} = (1, 1)$ and watch $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$.
screens.question: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{w}$. What is $\lambda$?

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{A}(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3(1, 1)$, so $(1, 1)$ is an eigenvector for 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ in the caption with $\mathbf{x}$ at $(1, 1)$.

byKey.one: 1 is the other factor's root. $\mathbf{A}(1, 1) = (3, 3)$, three times $\mathbf{w}$.
byKey.coords: You added the entries of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = (3, 3)$. $\lambda$ is the stretch factor: $(3, 3) = 3(1, 1)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = (3, 3)$ lies on the line of $\mathbf{w}$, three times as long. We found an eigenvector without solving $\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = 0$. A dependency among $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{v}$ was enough.

screens.title: A quarter turn
screens.prose: Now take the rotation $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 0)$. The canvas draws $\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v} = (0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{R}^2\mathbf{v} = (-1, 0)$.
screens.question: Which polynomial $p(z) = z^2 + cz + d$ has $p(\mathbf{R})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\mathbf{R}^2\mathbf{v}$ as a multiple of $\mathbf{v}$.

byKey.minus: You wrote $\mathbf{R}^2\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$. It is $-\mathbf{v}$: two quarter turns face the other way.

explain.text: $\mathbf{R}^2\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$, so $p(z) = z^2 + 1$. It has no real root, so no real factor $z - \lambda$. The search for a real eigenvector stops here.

screens.title: Factor over the complex numbers
screens.prose: Over $\mathbb{C}$, $i^2 = -1$, so $z^2 + 1 = (z - i)(z + i)$. For $z = a + bi$, $\bar z = a - bi$ and $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. The fundamental theorem of algebra: every non-constant complex polynomial is a product of linear factors.
screens.question: Then $(\mathbf{R} - i\mathbf{I})(\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. What is $\mathbf{w} = (\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}$?

hints.text: The first column of $\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I}$ is $(0 + i, 1 + 0)$.

feedback.correct: Right. The first column of $\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I}$ is $(i, 1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix}i&-1\\1&i\end{pmatrix}$; apply it to $(1, 0)$.

byKey.minus: You used $\mathbf{R} - i\mathbf{I}$. The factor applied first is $\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{I}$.
byKey.swap: You read a row, not the column. $(1, 0)$ picks out the first column, $(i, 1)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w} = (i, 1)$, and $\mathbf{R}(i, 1) = (-1, i)$. That is $i(i, 1)$, since $i \cdot i = -1$. So $\mathbf{R}$ has an eigenvector after all, in $\mathbb{C}^2$.

screens.title: Every real matrix?
screens.prose: A classmate says every real $2 \times 2$ matrix has a real eigenvalue, by the argument we just ran. Run it over $\mathbb{R}$ for $\mathbf{R}$. Drag $\mathbf{x}$: $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}$ never lies on the band.
screens.question: Which step fails over $\mathbb{R}$?

options.why: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are dependent over $\mathbb{R}$ too: $\mathbf{R}^2\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$.
$p(z) = z^2 + 1$ has degree 2, over any field.

options.text: A composition of injective maps is injective
options.why: That holds for maps over any field; it never used $\mathbb{C}$.

hints.text: Which step mentions the roots of $p$?
So the factoring line fails over $\mathbb{R}$.

feedback.correct: Right. $z^2 + 1$ has no real root, so it does not factor over $\mathbb{R}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the step that needs the roots of $p$.

byKey.dep: You blamed dependence. That step holds over $\mathbb{R}$; the factoring step is the one that needs $\mathbb{C}$.
byKey.inj: You blamed the composition step. It is fine; there is no real factor $z - \lambda$ to compose.

explain.text: Every other step works over $\mathbb{R}$. Factoring needs the fundamental theorem of algebra, which is a fact about $\mathbb{C}$. So the claim is false: $\mathbf{R}$ has no real eigenvalue, but it has $\pm i$.

screens.title: Every complex operator has an eigenvalue
screens.prose: Theorem (Axler 5.19). Let $V \ne \{\mathbf{0}\}$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and $T \in \mathcal{L}(V)$. Then $T$ has an eigenvalue. Take $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ and $n = \dim V$. $$a_0\mathbf{v} + a_1T\mathbf{v} + \cdots + a_nT^n\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$$ for some $a_k$ not all zero.
screens.question: Why do such $a_k$ exist?

options.text: $(\mathbf{v}, T\mathbf{v}, \dots, T^n\mathbf{v})$ has $n + 1$ vectors in a space of dimension $n$

options.why: That is what we are proving. Using it here would be circular.
$\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ is used later, to show $p$ is not constant. It makes nothing dependent.
That is false for most $T$: $\mathbf{A}^2 \ne \mathbf{0}$ in the hook.

feedback.correct: Right. A list longer than the dimension is dependent (level 1 l3).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the vectors in the list and compare with $\dim V$.

explain.text: $(\mathbf{v}, T\mathbf{v}, \dots, T^n\mathbf{v})$ has $n + 1$ entries in an $n$-dimensional space, so it is dependent. That gives a non-zero polynomial $p$ with $p(T)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. In the hook, $n = 2$ and $p(z) = z^2 - 4z + 3$.

screens.title: The proof, line by line
screens.prose: Order the proof of Axler 5.19. Each line carries its reason. One line is a tempting step that is wrong.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: The $n + 1$ vectors $\mathbf{v}, T\mathbf{v}, \dots, T^n\mathbf{v}$ are dependent, since $\dim V = n$ (level 1 l3).
So $p(T)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for some non-zero polynomial $p(z) = a_0 + a_1z + \cdots + a_nz^n$.
$p$ is not constant: otherwise $a_0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $a_0 \ne 0$, so $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$.
Over $\mathbb{C}$, $p(z) = c(z - \lambda_1)\cdots(z - \lambda_m)$ with $c \ne 0$, $m \ge 1$ (fundamental theorem of algebra).
So $(T - \lambda_1 I)\cdots(T - \lambda_m I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$: the composition is not injective.
A composition of injective maps is injective, so some $T - \lambda_j I$ is not, and $\lambda_j$ is an eigenvalue (level 2 l6). $\blacksquare$
Factor $p$ over $\mathbb{R}$ into factors $z - \lambda_j$, as $V$ may be real.
lines.why: $z^2 + 1$ has no real factors. The theorem needs $\mathbb{C}$, and the rotation shows why.

hints.text: After the polynomial: why it is not constant, then its factors.
End with the composition of injective maps.

feedback.correct: Right. Dependence, a non-constant polynomial, its complex factors, and one factor that is not injective.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $\mathbf{v}$, get the dependency, then the polynomial, then its factors.

byKey.x1: You factored over $\mathbb{R}$. That fails for $z^2 + 1$; the factoring line needs $\mathbb{C}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Dependence gives $p$, and $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ makes $p$ non-constant. Over $\mathbb{C}$ it splits into linear factors. Their composition kills $\mathbf{v}$, so one factor $T - \lambda_jI$ has a non-zero kernel.

screens.title: The lowest polynomial that kills v
screens.prose: `annihilating_poly(A, v)` returns the monic coefficients, highest degree first as `np.roots` wants, of the lowest-degree $p$ with $p(\mathbf{A})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. The starter returns `np.poly(A)`, the characteristic polynomial.
screens.question: Fix `annihilating_poly(A, v)`. Add $\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{v}$ to a list until `np.linalg.matrix_rank` stops growing, then solve by `np.linalg.lstsq`. Round to 6 places.

widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests: the hook, an eigenvector $(1, 1)$, the rotation and $\operatorname{diag}(1, 2, 3)$. Lists are compared exactly after rounding to 6 places. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Keep a list `K` that starts as `[v]`.
Append `A @ K[-1]` while the rank of the stacked list keeps growing.
Solve `K c = A^k v` with `lstsq`; the coefficients are `[1] + [-c_j]`, highest first.

feedback.correct: Right. The list stops growing at the first dependency, and that gives the lowest degree.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row.

byKey.test-2: For $\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)$ you returned degree 2. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}$ already, so $p(z) = z - 3$.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that `np.column_stack` gets a list of vectors.

explain.text:
When $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector the list stops after one vector, and $p$ has degree 1. Its degree is never above $n$, since $n + 1$ vectors are dependent.

```python
while True:
    nxt = A @ K[-1]
    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.column_stack(K + [nxt])) == len(K):
        break
    K.append(nxt)
```

screens.title: Cycles in an AR(2)
screens.prose: A spread follows the AR(2) model $x_t = x_{t-1} - 0.5x_{t-2}$. In state form, $(x_t, x_{t-1})$ is $\mathbf{C}(x_{t-1}, x_{t-2})$ with $\mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix}1&-0.5\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is $z^2 - z + 0.5$. The map $z \mapsto (a + bi)z$ shows what multiplying by a complex number does.
screens.question: Which eigenvalue of $\mathbf{C}$ has positive imaginary part?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $z^2 - z + 0.5 = 0$ by the quadratic formula; the discriminant is $-1$.

byKey.conj: That is the other root, with negative imaginary part. The two are conjugates, as for any real matrix.
byKey.real: You dropped the imaginary part. The discriminant $1 - 2 = -1$ gives $\pm 0.5i$.
byKey.noi: Divide the whole formula by 2: $\tfrac{1 \pm i}{2}$.

explain.text: $z = 0.5 \pm 0.5i$, with modulus $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.7071$ and angle $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Multiplying by it turns $z$ by $45°$ and shrinks it to 0.7071 of its length. Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix are how cycles appear in an AR or VAR model.

screens.title: How fast the cycle dies
screens.prose: Shock the spread once: $x_0 = 1$, $x_{-1} = 0$. Each step multiplies the state's eigen-coordinate by $0.5 + 0.5i$: a turn of $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ and a shrink by $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.7071$. So the cycle has period 8: the response crosses zero at $t = 3, 7, 11, 15$.
screens.question: After one full cycle, $x_8 = c\,x_0$. What is $c$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read $x_8$ on the chart, or raise 0.7071 to the 8th power.

byKey.one: 0.7071 is the shrink of one step. A full cycle takes 8 steps, so raise it to the 8th power.
byKey.half: You used 0.5, the real part, as the shrink: $0.5^8 \approx 0.0039$. The modulus is $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.7071$.
byKey.eighth: $x_6 = -0.125$ is two steps early. The cycle completes at $t = 8$.

explain.text: $(\sqrt{0.5})^8 = 0.5^4 = 0.0625$, and the chart shows $x_8 = 0.0625$. The angle sets the period, $2\pi / \tfrac{\pi}{4} = 8$ steps. The modulus sets the decay; below 1, a shock dies away while it cycles.

ideas: For $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ in an $n$-dimensional space, $(\mathbf{v}, T\mathbf{v}, \dots, T^n\mathbf{v})$ is dependent. So some non-constant $p$ has $p(T)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$.
Over $\mathbb{C}$, $p$ splits into factors $T - \lambda_j I$. One of them is not injective, so its $\lambda_j$ is an eigenvalue.
Over $\mathbb{R}$ the factoring can fail: the rotation has $p(z) = z^2 + 1$ and eigenvalues $\pm i$. An AR model with complex eigenvalues cycles.

formula.name: The key step
formula.note: Needs $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$, a complex space and finite dimension.

summary.trap: Not every real matrix has a real eigenvalue: the quarter turn has none. The proof needs $\mathbb{C}$ at the factoring line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the second entries: $i = \lambda \cdot 1$.

byKey.minus: $-i(i, 1) = (1, -i)$, not $(-1, i)$. Check the second entries.
byKey.one: $1 \cdot (i, 1) = (i, 1)$, not $(-1, i)$. Compare the second entries.

explain.text: The second entries give $\lambda = i$, and the first agree: $i \cdot i = -1$. So $i$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{R}$ over $\mathbb{C}$. Its conjugate $-i$ is the other, with eigenvector $(-i, 1)$.

quiz.prose: In the proof, $p(T)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for a non-zero polynomial $p$.
quiz.question: Why is $p$ not a non-zero constant $c$?

options.why: $p$ has degree at most $n$; its top coefficients may vanish, as for $(1, 1)$.
Nothing says $T$ is injective. The zero map is not.
The field plays no part here. $c\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $c \ne 0$ fails over any field.

feedback.correct: Right. A non-zero constant kills only $\mathbf{0}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would $p(T)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ say if $p = c$?

explain.text: If $p = c \ne 0$, then $p(T)\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Dividing by $c$ gives $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, a contradiction. So $p$ has degree at least 1, and it has a root over $\mathbb{C}$.

quiz.question: Why must one of $T - \lambda_1 I$, $T - \lambda_2 I$ fail to be injective?

options.text: If both were injective, so would their composition be; but it sends $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{0}$
Both must fail, since the product is zero
options.why: Only one need fail. For $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)$, $(\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I})(\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, yet $\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I}$ is injective.

options.text: The first one applied, $T - \lambda_2 I$, always fails
options.why: In $(\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I})(\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I})(1, 1) = \mathbf{0}$, the first factor applied is $\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I}$. It is injective; $\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I}$ fails.
That is the conclusion, not a reason. The proof avoids determinants.

feedback.correct: Right. Injective maps compose to an injective map.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would be true of the composition if both factors were injective?

byKey.first: You assumed the first factor applied fails. In $(\mathbf{A} - 3\mathbf{I})(\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I})(1, 1) = \mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I}$ is injective.

explain.text: If $S$ and $U$ are injective, $SU\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$. Here the composition kills $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$, so one factor is not injective. Its $\lambda_j$ is an eigenvalue.

quiz.prose: Let $T$ be multiplication by $x$ on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$, all real polynomials: $Tp = xp$. It has no eigenvalue, since $xp = \lambda p$ forces $p = 0$.
quiz.question: Which broken hypothesis is to blame for the missing eigenvalue?

options.text: Finite dimension: $1, x, x^2, \dots$ never become dependent

options.why: Over $\mathbb{C}$ it still has no eigenvalue: $xp = \lambda p$ forces $p = 0$ there too.
$x(p + q) = xp + xq$ and $x(cp) = c(xp)$: $T$ is linear.

feedback.correct: Right. The list $1, T1, T^21, \dots$ is $1, x, x^2, \dots$, independent for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which line of the proof needs $\dim V = n$?

explain.text: The proof needs $n + 1$ vectors to be dependent, which needs $\dim V = n$. In $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ the list $1, x, x^2, \dots$ stays independent. So no polynomial kills $1$, and the argument never starts.

quiz.question: What is the degree of the lowest-degree non-zero $p$ with $p(\mathbf{A})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is $(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})$ already dependent?

byKey.char: 2 is the degree of the characteristic polynomial. Here $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} - 3\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ already.
byKey.zero: A degree-0 $p$ is a non-zero constant, and $c\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{v}$ is already an eigenvector, so $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ is dependent. The lowest $p$ is $z - 3$, of degree 1. This is the edge case of the proof: one factor, one eigenvalue.
